selectInferToolkit

The selectInferToolkit package addresses a critical challenge in modern statistical modeling: conducting valid inference after performing model selection. In the era of big data and complex regression problems, researchers often employ model selection procedures like stepwise regression or penalized methods (e.g., lasso) to identify important variables. However, classical statistical inference assumes the model was chosen a priori—independent of the data. When this assumption is violated, standard statistical tests and confidence intervals can become overly optimistic, leading to unreliable conclusions.selectInferToolkit provides a user-friendly framework in R to facilitate post-selection inferential methods.

Installation

You can install the development version of selectInferToolkit like so:

devtools::install_github("petersonR/selectInferToolkit")

Package Overview

selectInferToolkit offers a comprehensive suite of tools, covering both model selection and the crucial post-selection inference steps.

Model Selection Methods

The package supports two broad classes of popular model selection techniques:

  • Stepwise Regression: Implement forward, backward, and bidirectional stepwise regression. User can use either the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) or the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) as selection criteria, leveraging the stepAIC function from the MASS package.
  • Penalized Regression: Perform lasso and elastic net regression with glmnet, or MCP, SCAD, and lasso regression with ncvreg. selectInferToolkit simplifies the process of obtaining models associated with either λmin\lambda_{min} or λ1se\lambda_{1se}.
    • λmin\lambda_{min} represents the regularization parameter λ\lambda that minimizes the cross-validation error, aiming for the best predictive performance.
    • λ1se\lambda_{1se} is a more conservative choice, selecting the largest λ\lambda where the cross-validation error is within one standard error of λmin\lambda_{min}. This often results in a sparser, more parsimonious model.

Post-Selection Inference Methods

The core contribution of selectInferToolkit lies in its ability to provide straightforward implementations of four post-selection inference methods, applicable after you’ve performed model selection using one of the methods above:

  1. UPSI: A baseline approach that performs no adjustment for the selection process. We refer to this as “unadjusted post-selection inference”, or “UPSI” for short. Others refer to this as “hybrid-OLS” (in the Gaussian outcome case).
  2. Bootstrap: A non-parametric bootstrap method that resamples data to account for selection uncertainty.
  3. Selective Inference: A theoretically grounded approach, currently available for lasso and forward stepwise selection through integration with the selectiveInference package.
  4. PIPE: [currently experimental]

Handling Non-Selected Variables

selectInferToolkit is explicit in its handling of non-selections. For infer_upsi() and infer_selective(), the nonselection argument can be set to:

  • Ignored: Treating non-selected variables as irrelevant.
  • Confident (point-mass) nulls: Assuming these variables have exactly zero effect.
  • Uncertain nulls: Aim to make inference on all variables but without the assumption that non-selections certainly have a null effect

The bootstrap handles non-selections through its inference_target and pad arguments instead (below), and PIPE gives inference for every variable. See ?infer_upsi for exactly what each nonselection mode returns.

Bootstrapping considerations

In bootstrapping, the selection is re-run on each resample and a non-selected coefficient is recorded as 0. The user specifies their inference_target as either "selections" or "all".

Recording non-selections as 0 makes the percentile interval of a small, rarely selected coefficient collapse toward [0,0][0, 0]. The pad argument corrects this. The default, pad = "zero_side", pushes the endpoints of any interval that contains 0 out to at least ±δ\pm\delta, a region of reasonably confident null that shrinks with nn (δ=γλ̂\delta = \gamma\hat\lambda for MCP/SCAD, k⋅SE\sqrt{k}\cdot\mathrm{SE} for stepwise IC); intervals that exclude 0 are unchanged. pad = "all" widens every interval by δ\delta (the valid choice for the lasso), and pad = "none" returns the raw percentile intervals (confident nulls). The radius is reported in the null_radius column.

Example

Let’s say you are wanting to predict gas mileage based on all variables in the mtcars data set.

library(selectInferToolkit)
#> Loading required package: broom
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

data("mtcars")

fit_full <- lm(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars)
summary(fit_full)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = mpg ~ ., data = mtcars)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
#> -3.4506 -1.6044 -0.1196  1.2193  4.6271 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)  
#> (Intercept) 12.30337   18.71788   0.657   0.5181  
#> cyl         -0.11144    1.04502  -0.107   0.9161  
#> disp         0.01334    0.01786   0.747   0.4635  
#> hp          -0.02148    0.02177  -0.987   0.3350  
#> drat         0.78711    1.63537   0.481   0.6353  
#> wt          -3.71530    1.89441  -1.961   0.0633 .
#> qsec         0.82104    0.73084   1.123   0.2739  
#> vs           0.31776    2.10451   0.151   0.8814  
#> am           2.52023    2.05665   1.225   0.2340  
#> gear         0.65541    1.49326   0.439   0.6652  
#> carb        -0.19942    0.82875  -0.241   0.8122  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 2.65 on 21 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.869,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.8066 
#> F-statistic: 13.93 on 10 and 21 DF,  p-value: 3.793e-07

Hmm, R2R^2 is high but nothing is “significant”. What is going on? The model is probably over-specified. Let’s use selectInferToolkit to narrow in on what we think the most important factors are. The select_stepwise_ic() function does forward selection via AIC by default (backward and bidirectional searches are available through direction).

Stepwise selection 

fit_aic <- select_stepwise_ic(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars, penalty = "AIC") 
fit_aic
#> Stepwise IC-based selector
#> 3 of 10 variables selected: hp, cyl, wt 
#> Meta information: family=gaussian, select_factors_together=FALSE, penalty=AIC, direction=forward, criterion=deviance, sigma_arg=NULL, sigma_used=NULL 
#> Default `infer()` method: boot

Functions prefixed with select_ create a selector class object. We can pass selector objects to coef, predict, and tidy() functions:

coef(fit_aic)
#> (Intercept)          wt         cyl          hp 
#>   20.090625   -3.098748   -1.681654   -1.236744
tidy(fit_aic)
#> # A tibble: 11 × 3
#>    term        selected  coef
#>    <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercept)        1 20.1 
#>  2 cyl                1 -1.68
#>  3 disp               0  0   
#>  4 hp                 1 -1.24
#>  5 drat               0  0   
#>  6 wt                 1 -3.10
#>  7 qsec               0  0   
#>  8 vs                 0  0   
#>  9 am                 0  0   
#> 10 gear               0  0   
#> 11 carb               0  0

Note that the predictors are standardized before selection, so by default these coefficients are the change in mpg per standard deviation of each predictor. Use tidy(fit_aic, scale_coef = FALSE) for per-unit effects (see ?tidy.selector).

So we find that AIC selects wt, cyl, and hp. But where are the p-values?!

This is where post-selection inference comes in; p-values that do not adjust for the selective process will be too small. Again, we call this “unadjusted post-selection inference” (or UPSI, for short).

fit_aic_infer_upsi <- infer_upsi(fit_aic, data = mtcars)
fit_aic_infer_upsi
#> Unadjusted Post-Selection Inference (UPSI) inference applied post Stepwise IC-based Selection 
#> 3 of 10 variables selected. 
#> Nonselections were considered ignored 
#> Meta information: none 
#> Median CI length = 3; mean = 2.9; max = 3.9
tidy(fit_aic_infer_upsi) %>% dplyr::filter(selected == 1)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 7
#>   term        selected  coef estimate ci_low ci_high  p_value
#>   <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)        1 20.1     20.1   19.2   21.0   9.94e-28
#> 2 cyl                1 -1.68    -1.68  -3.61   0.247 9.85e- 2
#> 3 hp                 1 -1.24    -1.24  -2.83   0.359 1.40e- 1
#> 4 wt                 1 -3.10    -3.10  -4.52  -1.68  1.99e- 4

Thus, wt is significant! We know this confidence interval may be biased and too precise, as we’ve used the data both to select the model and now are using the same data to perform inference (UPSI!). What if we wanted to adjust our uncertainty quantification for the selective process?

Each selection process has a default infer method that is, for the most part, not an UPSI method. The default for stepwise selection via information criteria is bootstrapping. The code below is equivalent to calling infer_boot.

set.seed(1)
fit_aic_infer_boot <- infer(fit_aic, data = mtcars, B = 100)
#> Default inference method is bootstrapping (infer_boot). This may take a moment. Set a seed for reproducibility, or use infer_upsi() / infer_selective() for faster alternatives.
#> Bootstrapping with B = 100 replicates...
fit_aic_infer_boot
#> Bootstrap inference applied post Stepwise IC-based Selection 
#> 3 of 10 variables selected. 
#> Nonselections were considered N/A 
#> Meta information: B=100, inference_target=selections, pad=zero_side 
#> Median CI length = 7.9; mean = 7.6; max = 10
tidy(fit_aic_infer_boot) 
#> # A tibble: 11 × 8
#>    term        selected  coef estimate ci_low ci_high prop_selected null_radius
#>    <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>         <dbl>       <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercept)        1 20.1    20.2    18.2    22.6           1          NA   
#>  2 cyl                1 -1.68   -0.386  -4.07    5.15          0.5         2.64
#>  3 disp               0  0      NA      NA      NA            NA           3.13
#>  4 hp                 1 -1.24   -0.834  -4.48    2.18          0.43        2.11
#>  5 drat               0  0      NA      NA      NA            NA           1.24
#>  6 wt                 1 -3.10   -3.28   -7.34    2.62          0.91        2.62
#>  7 qsec               0  0      NA      NA      NA            NA           1.85
#>  8 vs                 0  0      NA      NA      NA            NA           1.50
#>  9 am                 0  0      NA      NA      NA            NA           1.45
#> 10 gear               0  0      NA      NA      NA            NA           1.56
#> 11 carb               0  0      NA      NA      NA            NA           1.89

These results are less promising. Here we can also use a wrapper for the selectiveInference method. Selective inference for stepwise selection conditions on the Mallows-Cp form of the criterion, so we select with criterion = "cp" to make the selection and the inference agree (with the default criterion = "deviance", the two can stop at different steps, and infer_selective() warns and falls back to conditioning on a fixed number of steps):

fit_aic_cp <- select_stepwise_ic(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars, penalty = "AIC", criterion = "cp")
fit_aic_SI <- infer_selective(fit_aic_cp, data = mtcars)
fit_aic_SI 
#> Selective inference applied post Stepwise IC-based Selection 
#> 3 of 10 variables selected. 
#> Nonselections were considered ignored 
#> Meta information: conditioning=aic 
#> Median CI length = Inf; mean = Inf; max = Inf
tidy(fit_aic_SI) 
#> # A tibble: 11 × 7
#>    term        selected  coef estimate ci_low ci_high p_value
#>    <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercept)        1 20.1     NA      NA     NA     NA    
#>  2 cyl                1 -1.68    -1.68 -Inf     30.4    0.235
#>  3 disp               0  0       NA      NA     NA     NA    
#>  4 hp                 1 -1.24    -1.24  -25.5  Inf      0.795
#>  5 drat               0  0       NA      NA     NA     NA    
#>  6 wt                 1 -3.10    -3.10  -11.6    5.87   0.224
#>  7 qsec               0  0       NA      NA     NA     NA    
#>  8 vs                 0  0       NA      NA     NA     NA    
#>  9 am                 0  0       NA      NA     NA     NA    
#> 10 gear               0  0       NA      NA     NA     NA    
#> 11 carb               0  0       NA      NA     NA     NA

Here we see that after adjusting for the selective process, we are unable to claim significance of any of these effects, and the CIs are very wide (some are infinite).

Lastly, as stated above, infer_upsi() and infer_selective() provide three approaches to handling non-selections: ignored (ignoring them), confident_nulls (treating them as confident (point-mass) degenerate nulls at zero), and uncertain_nulls (treating them as uncertain). For details about each of these, see ?infer_upsi.

Penalized regression

Lasso via glmnet

We can also try selecting the most important factors are by penalized models. We can fit the lasso with cross validation and selects coefficients associated with the best predicting model (default, i.e. lambda.min) or the most compact model that predicts about as well as the best model, i.e. lambda.1se.

set.seed(12)
fit_lso <- select_glmnet(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) 
fit_lso 
#> Penalized `glmnet`-based selector
#> 5 of 10 variables selected: carb, am, hp, cyl, wt 
#> Meta information: family=gaussian, lambda=best, lambda_used=0.543, cv_info=list(...), ellipses=list(...), alpha=1 
#> Default `infer()` method: selective
tidy(fit_lso)
#> # A tibble: 11 × 3
#>    term        selected    coef
#>    <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercept)        1 20.1   
#>  2 cyl                1 -1.56  
#>  3 disp               0  0     
#>  4 hp                 1 -0.956 
#>  5 drat               0  0     
#>  6 wt                 1 -2.66  
#>  7 qsec               0  0     
#>  8 vs                 0  0     
#>  9 am                 1  0.169 
#> 10 gear               0  0     
#> 11 carb               1 -0.0934

The lasso selects the same 3 variables as stepwise AIC, plus am and carb (with small coefficients). The lasso alone does not provide any p-value or CI to do inference, but UPSIs aside we can again perform a (questionable) hybrid inferential process where ordinary least squares theory is used for inference as though we never used the data for selection.

fit_lasso_infer_upsi <-infer_upsi(fit_lso, data = mtcars) 
tidy(fit_lasso_infer_upsi)
#> # A tibble: 11 × 7
#>    term        selected    coef estimate ci_low ci_high   p_value
#>    <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercept)        1 20.1      20.1   19.2    21.0    2.67e-26
#>  2 cyl                1 -1.56     -1.46  -3.51    0.588  1.74e- 1
#>  3 disp               0  0        NA     NA      NA     NA       
#>  4 hp                 1 -0.956    -1.08  -3.24    1.08   3.37e- 1
#>  5 drat               0  0        NA     NA      NA     NA       
#>  6 wt                 1 -2.66     -2.31  -4.12   -0.500  1.90e- 2
#>  7 qsec               0  0        NA     NA      NA     NA       
#>  8 vs                 0  0        NA     NA      NA     NA       
#>  9 am                 1  0.169     1.04  -0.470   2.54   1.89e- 1
#> 10 gear               0  0        NA     NA      NA     NA       
#> 11 carb               1 -0.0934   -0.815 -2.30    0.666  2.91e- 1

These results are close to the UPSI results for stepwise AIC, since the two selected models share cyl, hp, and wt; wt is still seemingly significant.

Selective inference

fit_lasso_infer_SI <- infer_selective(fit_lso, data = mtcars)
tidy(fit_lasso_infer_SI)
#> # A tibble: 11 × 7
#>    term        selected    coef estimate ci_low ci_high  p_value
#>    <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercept)        1 20.1      NA      NA     NA     NA      
#>  2 cyl                1 -1.56     -1.46   -6.90   2.72   0.204  
#>  3 disp               0  0        NA      NA     NA     NA      
#>  4 hp                 1 -0.956    -1.08  -20.6    3.78   0.157  
#>  5 drat               0  0        NA      NA     NA     NA      
#>  6 wt                 1 -2.66     -2.31  -13.3   -0.569  0.00873
#>  7 qsec               0  0        NA      NA     NA     NA      
#>  8 vs                 0  0        NA      NA     NA     NA      
#>  9 am                 1  0.169     1.04  -13.6    2.25   0.710  
#> 10 gear               0  0        NA      NA     NA     NA      
#> 11 carb               1 -0.0934   -0.815  -2.20  24.2    0.834

Here we see that after adjusting for the selective process with selective inference, we are able to assert a significant effect of wt even after the selective process, though its CI is considerably wider than the UPSI interval.

Bootstrapping

The lasso’s bias does not vanish for large effects, so for a lasso selector the uniformly valid choice is to pad every interval by λ̂\hat\lambda:

set.seed(1)
fit_lasso_infer_boot <- infer_boot(fit_lso, data = mtcars, B = 100, inference_target = "all", pad = "all") 
#> Bootstrapping with B = 100 replicates...
tidy(fit_lasso_infer_boot) 
#> # A tibble: 11 × 8
#>    term       selected    coef estimate ci_low ci_high prop_selected null_radius
#>    <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>         <dbl>       <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercep…        1 20.1     20.1    19.3    21.0            1         NA    
#>  2 cyl               1 -1.56    -1.15   -3.39    0.543          0.85       0.543
#>  3 disp              0  0       -0.0570 -1.28    0.543          0.08       0.543
#>  4 hp                1 -0.956   -0.901  -2.80    0.543          0.85       0.543
#>  5 drat              0  0        0.278  -0.543   1.87           0.48       0.543
#>  6 wt                1 -2.66    -2.45   -4.46   -0.293          1          0.543
#>  7 qsec              0  0        0.106  -0.543   1.31           0.18       0.543
#>  8 vs                0  0        0.0973 -0.543   1.27           0.28       0.543
#>  9 am                1  0.169    0.320  -0.543   1.98           0.5        0.543
#> 10 gear              0  0        0.0300 -0.543   0.940          0.1        0.543
#> 11 carb              1 -0.0934  -0.286  -1.75    0.543          0.63       0.543

Compare these to the raw percentile intervals (pad = "none"), where coefficients that are rarely selected collapse toward [0,0][0, 0]:

set.seed(1)
fit_lasso_infer_boot <- infer_boot(fit_lso, data = mtcars, B = 100, inference_target = "all", pad = "none") 
#> Bootstrapping with B = 100 replicates...
tidy(fit_lasso_infer_boot) 
#> # A tibble: 11 × 8
#>    term       selected    coef estimate ci_low ci_high prop_selected null_radius
#>    <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>         <dbl>       <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercep…        1 20.1     20.1    19.3    21.0            1             NA
#>  2 cyl               1 -1.56    -1.15   -2.85    0              0.85          NA
#>  3 disp              0  0       -0.0570 -0.740   0              0.08          NA
#>  4 hp                1 -0.956   -0.901  -2.26    0              0.85          NA
#>  5 drat              0  0        0.278   0       1.33           0.48          NA
#>  6 wt                1 -2.66    -2.45   -3.92   -0.837          1             NA
#>  7 qsec              0  0        0.106   0       0.769          0.18          NA
#>  8 vs                0  0        0.0973  0       0.729          0.28          NA
#>  9 am                1  0.169    0.320   0       1.44           0.5           NA
#> 10 gear              0  0        0.0300  0       0.397          0.1           NA
#> 11 carb              1 -0.0934  -0.286  -1.21    0              0.63          NA

For a more in depth tutorial and examples for different methods, please consult the package vignette.

MCP via ncvreg 

set.seed(12)
fit_mcp <- select_ncvreg(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) 
fit_mcp 
#> Penalized `ncvreg`-based selector
#> 3 of 10 variables selected: am, qsec, wt

#> Default `infer()` method: boot
tidy(fit_mcp)
#> # A tibble: 11 × 3

Bootstrapping

MCP is unbiased for large effects, so the default zero-side padding applies: intervals that contain 0 are padded out to ±γλ̂\pm\gamma\hat\lambda, and the others are left alone.

set.seed(12)
fit_mcp_infer_boot <- infer_boot(fit_mcp, data = mtcars, B = 100, inference_target = "all") 
#> Bootstrapping with B = 100 replicates...
tidy(fit_mcp_infer_boot) 
#> # A tibble: 11 × 8
#>    term        selected  coef estimate ci_low ci_high prop_selected null_radius
#>    <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>         <dbl>       <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercept)        1 20.1   20.1     19.2    21.2           1          NA   
#>  2 cyl                0  0     -0.801   -3.42    1.02          0.33        1.02
#>  3 disp               0  0     -0.209   -3.24    1.02          0.07        1.02
#>  4 hp                 0  0     -0.396   -3.98    1.02          0.11        1.02
#>  5 drat               0  0      0.378   -1.02    2.18          0.22        1.02
#>  6 wt                 1 -3.83  -2.83    -5.73    1.02          0.79        1.02
#>  7 qsec               1  2.19   1.01    -1.02    4.11          0.52        1.02
#>  8 vs                 0  0     -0.0886  -2.59    1.02          0.08        1.02
#>  9 am                 1  1.46   0.763   -1.02    3.20          0.38        1.02
#> 10 gear               0  0      0.133   -1.02    1.77          0.14        1.02
#> 11 carb               0  0     -0.710   -3.57    1.02          0.52        1.02
set.seed(12)
fit_mcp_infer_boot <- infer_boot(fit_mcp, data = mtcars, B = 100, inference_target = "all", pad = "none") 
#> Bootstrapping with B = 100 replicates...
tidy(fit_mcp_infer_boot) 
#> # A tibble: 11 × 8
#>    term        selected  coef estimate ci_low ci_high prop_selected null_radius
#>    <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>         <dbl>       <dbl>
#>  1 (Intercept)        1 20.1   20.1     19.2   21.2            1             NA
#>  2 cyl                0  0     -0.801   -3.42   0              0.33          NA
#>  3 disp               0  0     -0.209   -3.24   0              0.07          NA
